title: WUSH: Near-Optimal Adaptive Transforms for LLM Quantization
claim: Fixed or whitening transforms can raise quantization error for some points; combining a Hadamard backbone with data-adaptive scaling lowers it.
layout: 6x4 grid of 2-D toy plots, rows are transforms, shared legend below
description: A 6-row by 4-column grid of small 2-D toy plots. Columns are FP (original space), FP (transformed space), INT (original space) and INT (transformed space). Rows are transforms: Identity T=I, Hadamard T=H, Calibrated Hadamard T=HU^T, Whitening T=S^-1U^T, WUS T=S^-1/2U^T, and WUSH T=HS^-1/2U^T, which is the proposed method. Each panel shows a black ellipse for the data distribution, a tilted dotted basis grid, and two green example points. Translucent green boxes mark each point's noise zone, and green circles give its expected error. The INT panels carry a blue-white-red heatmap of the change in expected error, with dashed equilibrium lines. Whitening turns the ellipse into a circle and produces large red error regions. A boxed legend across the bottom explains the symbols. The eye goes first to the colorful heatmaps and the bottom row.
caption: Compute WUSH and Pre-Quantize Weights
abstract: Quantizing LLM weights and activations is a standard approach for efficient deployment, but a few extreme outliers can stretch the dynamic range and amplify low-bit quantization errors. Prior transform-based mitigations (e.g., Hadamard rotations) are fixed and data-agnostic, and their optimality for quantization has remained unclear. We derive closed-form optimal linear blockwise transforms for joint weight-activation quantization under standard RTN AbsMax-scaled block quantizers, covering both integer and floating-point formats. The resulting construction, WUSH, combines a Hadamard backbone with a data-dependent second-moment component to form a non-orthogonal transform that is provably near-optimal for FP and INT quantizers under mild assumptions while admitting an efficient fused GPU implementation. Empirically, WUSH improves W4A4 accuracy over the strongest Hadamard-based baselines (e.g., on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct in MXFP4, it gains +2.8 average points with RTN and +0.7 with GPTQ) while delivering up to 5.8$\times$ per-layer throughput over BF16 via FP4 MatMul. Source code is available at https://github.com/IST-DASLab/WUSH.
